notable_claims: The item addresses the technical or ethical ability to cancel posts authored by others on Usenet.
classification.summary: A newsgroup post forwarded by Carl M. Kadie regarding the policy of canceling articles posted by other users. The discussion takes place within the comp.admin.policy newsgroup.

notable_claims: Institutional control of campus facilities should not be used as a device of censorship.
System administrators who expel students without formal hearings should face disciplinary action.
Computer policies that contradict general university policy are null and void.
organizations: University of Illinois, Dept. of Comp. Sci.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues that university computer policies must align with general institutional policies regarding due process and free expression. He contends that system administrators should be subject to disciplinary action if they expel students without a formal hearing. He asserts that any computer policy contradicting broader university standards of academic freedom is null and void.
classification.title: Re: Canceling someone else's article

notable_claims: Due process provides disgruntled users with a nondestructive path and keeps policy enforcers honest.
User participation in formulating policy increases the perceived legitimacy of those policies.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the necessity of due process and student participation in the creation of university computer policies. The author argues that peer representation on policy committees provides legitimacy and protects users, countering claims that such committees are merely composed of compliant students.
classification.title: Re: Due process and computer policies (was OSU Policies)

notable_claims: Computing privileges should not be suspended pending a formal expulsion hearing unless safety is at risk.
Disciplinary records for computer infractions should remain separate from academic transcripts.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the due process rights of students facing expulsion from university computer systems. The author cites the Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students to argue against suspending computing privileges before a hearing and against placing disciplinary records on academic transcripts.

notable_claims: Undergraduates were prohibited from posting or emailing off campus.
Policy enforcement was described by a sysadmin as a 'weapon' against specific users.
The CIS policies lacked formal due process or hearing mechanisms for system expulsion.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie critiques the Computer and Information Services (CIS) policies at Ohio State University. He highlights concerns regarding selective enforcement of email restrictions for undergraduates and a lack of due process for users facing system suspension. The post notes that censorship is justified by vague obligations to network operators without citing specific contracts.
classification.title: Ohio State University CIS Policies

identity.subject: Re: Ohio State University CIS Policies

notable_claims: Lack of clear due process in CIS policies can lead to administrative run-arounds when students are locked out of systems.
Local system administrators may be discouraged from solving access problems at the local level.
classification.summary: A student at Ohio State University describes the difficulty of regaining access to a locked class account. The author details a bureaucratic struggle involving multiple administrators and the University Ombudsperson, illustrating the practical consequences of lacking clear due process in computer system policies.
classification.title: Re: Ohio State University CIS Policies

identity.subject: Re: Ohio State University CIS Policies

notable_claims: University sexual harassment rules and state laws on pornography are used to justify restricting publicly readable adult images.
Disk quota enforcement is prioritized based on the relevance of files to computer science instruction.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the intersection of university sexual harassment rules and state laws concerning pornography on campus computer systems. The author explains that while private files are generally ignored, publicly readable adult images are restricted to avoid legal liability and protect minors. Additionally, disk quota enforcement is described as being based on the educational purpose of the system rather than content censorship.
classification.title: publicly-readable "adult" gifs

notable_claims: University rules and state law combined to dictate policies on adult content.
There is a distinction between public access to files and the act of sexual harassment.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the intersection of university rules and state law concerning the hosting of adult imagery on campus computer systems. The participants debate whether public file permissions for such content constitute sexual harassment under institutional policy.
